If two Playwright tests share a browser context around "API and UI contract alignment — Architecture review", you do not have a test suite. You have a time bomb.

Playwright  ·  API and UI contract alignment — Architecture review

How the suite actually sees this
API and UI contract alignment — Architecture review is a query contract, not a node you cache. Locator re-runs against the live DOM; ElementHandle dies on re-render. One BrowserContext per test, storageState for auth, auto-wait instead of sleep. Use real Playwright APIs, lifecycle boundaries, isolation rules, observability artifacts, and CI behavior. Explain what is deterministic, what is flaky, and which design decision protects test signal. Focus on architecture review: state invariants, boundary decisions, extension points, and the questions a technical lead should ask. Write with a tech-lead point of view, one concrete production lesson, and no filler.

For "API and UI contract alignment — Architecture review", which isolation model would you actually ship?

A) On API and UI contract alignment — Architecture review: One shared browser + shared cookies for speed
B) On API and UI contract alignment — Architecture review: One browser context per test, storageState for auth, zero shared mutable cookies
C) On API and UI contract alignment — Architecture review: Login UI in every test because it is more "real"
D) On API and UI contract alignment — Architecture review: Disable parallelism so order-dependent tests pass

Drop A, B, C or D.
The call — and why it holds on API and UI contract alignment — Architecture review — is in the comments.

How you can apply this
Map "API and UI contract alignment — Architecture review" to one process chain — not 200 loose terms.
Explain the workflow out loud: locator query → auto-wait → assert → trace on fail. That is understanding, not rote.
Rehearse one PRD miss under a timer.
Keep a one-line playbook: what broke, first t-code or API, the standard you shipped.
Pattern recognition + practice + a clean story. That is what interviews and PRD both test.

Your tool is probably not the problem. I know, blaming the tool is tempting.

Jira feels painful, so we look at Linear.
Releases are messy, so we rethink the branching strategy.
Tests are flaky, so maybe Cypress is the problem and Playwright will save us.
CI is slow, so we start talking about rebuilding the pipeline.

Now we do the same thing with AI.
Development feels too slow? Add Copilot. Add agents. Generate more code. Automate more of the workflow. And sometimes that genuinely helps.

But I think we skip a question far too often: Why did we need the tool in the first place?
What problem were we actually trying to solve?

Because changing the tool without understanding that usually means carrying the same process into a new place. I see teams do exactly that.

A messy backlog does not suddenly become useful because the UI is nicer.
Painful deployments do not become safe because the CI platform changed.
Moving to trunk-based development does not give you continuous delivery if the team still works in huge batches and does not trust its tests.

And AI is not going to fix unclear requirements, weak reviews, poor testing, or bad architectural decisions either. It can absolutely help you write more code. Faster, too.
But more code was not necessarily the problem. That distinction matters.

I’m not saying teams should never change tools. Sometimes the current tool really is holding you back. But before migrating everything, I’d look at the process first.

Otherwise, you can spend weeks replacing the tool and eventually realize you rebuilt the same problems around it. The interface changed. The workflow got shinier. The habits stayed exactly the same.

elements.content:
My test suite was green for weeks. Then one flaky failure exposed a lie my rollback strategy had been telling me.

Here is what happened.

I built my MySQL test fixture the textbook way. Open a transaction before each test, run the test, roll back after. No cleanup scripts, no truncating tables, no leftover state. Fast and clean.

Or so I thought.

One test kept failing intermittently. A user count assertion expected 0 rows but sometimes found 1. Only sometimes. The worst kind of bug.

I spent an afternoon assuming it was a race condition in my parallel test runner. It was not.

The real culprit was an AFTER INSERT trigger on the users table. Every time a user was inserted, the trigger wrote an audit row into an audit_log table.

Here is the part that broke my brain. In MySQL with InnoDB, a trigger runs inside the same transaction as the statement that fired it. My rollback SHOULD have wiped both rows.

But the trigger did not just write a row. It called a stored procedure that ran an explicit COMMIT.

⚠️ That single COMMIT ended my test transaction early. Everything after it ran in autocommit mode. My fixture rollback at the end had nothing left to roll back.

The orphaned audit row survived. The next test in sequence found that poisoned row and failed its assertion.

Three things I confirmed the hard way:

1. A COMMIT or ROLLBACK inside a stored procedure or trigger terminates your outer transaction silently. MySQL does not warn you.

2. DDL statements like CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE cause an implicit commit too. If your code under test runs schema changes, your isolation is already gone.

3. Transactional fixtures give you a false sense of safety. They only protect the transactions they actually control.

My fix was blunt but honest. For tests that touch trigger-heavy tables, I dropped the transaction rollback approach and switched to explicit truncation of every affected table in teardown.

Slower. Uglier. But deterministic.

The lesson I keep repeating to myself now: test isolation is not something your framework guarantees. It is something your database schema either allows or quietly sabotages.

Save this for your next project. When your rollback fixture starts leaking state, check for triggers and procedures that commit behind your back.

Most "self-healing CI" demos stop at "the AI found the bug." The harder problem is: when do you let it fix something automatically, and when do you force a human to look?
I built a multi-agent system that watches CI pipelines, classifies failures, and only auto-fixes the categories where there's an objectively correct answer:
🔍 Triage Agent — classifies root cause (infra_flaky / dependency_issue / app_bug) with confidence, via LLM
🔧 Remediation Agent — proposes a fix, but ONLY a mechanical revert of a dependency file changed in the last commit. Never generates code. Never touches app_bug — "the test expected 5, got 6" needs a human who knows intended behavior, not a guess.
🛡️ Governance Agent — 5 independent checks before any fix goes out: global kill switch, per-repo default-deny, category allowlist, confidence floor, blast-radius limit. Every check logs its reasoning either way.
📨 Notifier Agent — opens a PR if approved, flags flaky if it's not a real bug, opens a diagnosis Issue (tagging the likely dev) otherwise.
Built with zero agent framework — the whole thing is plain Python, on purpose. I wanted to understand what LangGraph/ADK actually abstract away before reaching for either.
So I also wrote up how the exact same design maps onto both, in the README — including a trade-off I didn't expect going in: the hand-rolled version enforces "governance always runs" in code (nothing else executes if it doesn't). Port it to a single-agent-with-tools ADK design, and that guarantee moves into the prompt instead — the model has to remember to call the governance tool. An instruction is not a boundary.

SDLC isn’t dead. It’s getting instrumented.

Cloudflare just proposed an Agent Development Lifecycle, and OpenAI shipped GPT-6 Astra tuned for computer use and coding.

Astra scored 57.9% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 74.1% on DeepSWE v1.1.

As an AI engineer, I like the direction. But ADLC only works if our fundamentals are strong: evaluation, permissions, observability, and rollback.

Cloudflare’s ADLC frames software as an automated factory where agents handle testing, deployment, and maintenance. That can remove real bottlenecks. The risk is obvious too: agents move faster than humans, so bad decisions propagate faster.

A lesson I learned while building production systems is that the gap between a demo and a production system comes down to how you test, approve, and recover. At Proxify, Paxful, and care.coach we got value from LLMs and agents only after we treated them like any service in the stack, not magic.

What changes with ADLC + Astra-level agents:
- Shift from “human executes” to “agent proposes, human approves” on critical paths. Keep the human-in-the-loop until metrics prove otherwise.
- Treat LLM evaluation like unit tests. Define pass/fail on tasks, not vibes. Track drift.
- Identity and blast radius first. Agents get least privilege, time-bound tokens, and environment fences.
- Full observability for agent actions. Logs, traces, prompts, tools called, artifacts changed. Reproducible runs.
- Rollback as a first-class path. Every agent action is versioned and reversible.

Practical starting points I’d trust today:
- Agents triaging flaky tests and suggesting fixes, not committing code.
- Agents drafting infra changes as PRs with inline reasoning, not merging.
- Agents running RAG evaluations nightly and opening issues when quality drops.

After working on these systems, my biggest takeaway is simple: AI Engineering is still engineering. ADLC doesn’t replace discipline. It makes the cost of skipping it immediate and visible.

If you could give agents one permission in your stack today, what would it be, and which metric would gate it?

I published a documentary with 45 of its 62 on-camera shots out of sync. I had a test for that failure. It passed.

It wasn't flaky. The test did exactly what it was written to do, on the file it was written to look at, and that file was not the film.

For context: I make documentaries with AI and nobody films anything. A script is written, a voice reads it, software finds an archival photo per line, a video model animates some, and a synthetic on-camera presenter is generated shot by shot. The pipeline runs mostly unattended; deciding whether it's good is still mine. Eleven films in about three weeks on two GPUs at home.

The bug was banal: the assembler placed each shot's picture at the first spoken word, while each take was aligned to the start of its audio file, which begins with a little silence. The picture was always late, and the error lived in the assembly that nothing measured.
What actually bothered me is that I had written the rule months earlier: measure the delivered film, not the takes. I never wired it to anything that runs.

None of this is interesting because it removes people. It gets interesting when the output is dependable enough that someone can use it, a much harder bar than getting one good clip out of a model. So I rebuilt around one idea: if a lesson cannot run, it is not in the system. 62 checks now, each carrying the incident that caused it, 463 unit tests underneath, and every measurement kept rather than just pass or fail, because a generative pipeline does not fail the same way twice and the shape of a run tells you more than its verdict.

After the rebuild, going through a cut by hand, I found fourteen shots that slipped past the blocker. When a take is unusable a repair swaps in a held still, and that swap removed the shot from the check's list so it came back green. I found the first one by eye, 39 seconds in. The fix was not a better blocker but a second one watching for beats demoted out of the first one's view.

This is the last in the series for a while. I am starting a full-time role working on AI video, which I'm very excited about it. More next week.

I've been going down a rabbit hole this week on Claude Fable 5, GPT-6 Astra, and Jev.

My first instinct was to compare them head to head. Turns out that's the wrong way to look at it.

Fable and Astra are doers. They write features, refactor code and run long agentic tasks. Fable leans toward long, autonomous coding work. Astra is strong at computer use, driving browsers and apps that don't have APIs. Both cost around $10 in / $50 out per 1M tokens.

Jev is a decider. It doesn't write anything, not even code. You give it some data and a fixed list of answers, and it picks one with a confidence score. Around $0.04 per 1M input tokens, output free, and it answers in milliseconds.

My first question was: can I use it for coding or manual testing?

Not directly. It can't write code, and it can't click through an app like a tester. But it can handle the small decisions around that work:
→ Which area does this bug belong to?
→ Is this test failure flaky or real?
→ Does this PR need a deep review or a quick look?
→ Which test cases should run first for this change?

In our AIDLC setup, a surprising number of the AI calls I trigger are exactly these kinds of tiny decisions, and today they go through big, expensive models. A decision model could take those, and leave the real building to Fable or Astra.

What I'm still unsure about:
• Jev is about a week old and in early access
• The speed and cost numbers are from the vendor, not independent tests
• I haven't seen its security or compliance details yet

So I'm not rushing to swap anything. But I'm definitely keeping an eye on it.

My takeaway as an engineer: the skill isn't just knowing how to prompt a model anymore. It's knowing which kind of model a task actually needs.

Has anyone tried Jev yet? What did you use it for? 👇

🚀 Elevating Playwright Automation: Lessons from a Flight Booking System


While optimizing the test suite for a complex ticket booking system, I was reminded of a core principle: Never let environment or browser-specific logic clutter your actual test scripts.


Conditional skips inside tests might work for smaller suites, but as your project grows, it quickly becomes a maintenance bottleneck. Moving test execution management from the code level to the Configuration & Tagging level is a game-changer.


Here are 4 key practices we implemented to keep our automation clean, scalable, and resilient:


1️⃣ Leverage Tagging over Hardcoded Logic
Instead of writing conditional logic inside test blocks (like skipping WebKit during payment gateway checks), use metadata tags (@smoke, @chromium-only, @flaky):


TypeScript
test('confirm ticket reservation @webkit-skip', async ({ page }) => {   // test execution }); 
Now, your CI/CD pipeline or CLI commands handle what runs and what doesn't:
npx playwright test --grep-invert @webkit-skip


2️⃣ Manage Browsers via playwright.config.ts
Scattering test.skip(browserName === 'webkit') across multiple files creates technical debt. Instead, centralize cross-browser rules inside playwright.config.ts. Use Playwright’s Projects feature to cleanly map specific directories or user flows (e.g., seat selection, payment processing) to dedicated browser profiles.


3️⃣ Link Skipped Tests directly to Tickets
If a test must be skipped or marked as fixme, enforce a strict rule: Always link the issue ticket ID.


TypeScript
test.fixme(isCI, 'Ticket #BOOK-1234: Payment gateway timeout in staging'); 
This simple habit prevents disabled tests from being forgotten in the repository indefinitely.


4️⃣ Quarantine Flaky Tests
A flaky booking confirmation test shouldn't just be hidden with a quick skip. Isolate flaky tests into a dedicated Quarantine Pipeline or configure Playwright's retries to capture actionable trace logs and metrics without blocking release gates.


💡 Key Takeaway:


"Using test.skip works, but for large-scale enterprise projects, leveraging Tagging and playwright.config.ts decouples test scripts from environment logic—giving full control back to your CI/CD pipelines."

The Chilean sea bass on fancy restaurant menus started out as an ugly deep sea fish called the Patagonian toothfish that almost nobody in America wanted to eat.

Before 1977 the name Chilean sea bass didn't even exist. That year a fish wholesaler named Lee Lantz came across the toothfish in Chile and figured the white flaky meat could sell back home, but he knew nobody was going to order something called a toothfish.

So he gave it a new name, trying out Pacific sea bass and South American sea bass before he landed on Chilean sea bass for the exact same fish. He kept the word bass because it reads familiar and premium and he added Chilean because it reads specific and a little exotic.

It isn't even a bass (it's a cod family fish) and most of it doesn't come from Chile, but the FDA accepted the made up name as an official market name in 1994 and by the mid 1990s the catch was up more than 30 times from its starting level.

Marketers call this the Country of Origin Effect, where a place name attached to a product makes it feel more premium than the identical thing without it.

If you run a business the easiest place to test this is the name and category line at the top of your ads and landing page. Write a second version that puts the exact same product in a category your buyer already pays more for (or names a specific origin that's actually true), then run both against the same audience and budget and watch your cost per purchase and average order value.

Nothing about the fish ever changed except the name, so what are you selling right now that's priced like a toothfish when it should be priced like a Chilean sea bass?

What I would tell anyone starting their first developer job, having watched several students start theirs.

Weeks one to two — your job is questions, not output. There is a window where asking anything is free, and it closes faster than you think. Use it on the things that are embarrassing to ask about in month four. Why do we deploy this way. What does this acronym mean. Who decides this.

Weeks six to ten — find the thing nobody owns. Every team has one. A flaky test everyone reruns, a deploy step that is manual for no reason, documentation that lies. Fix it without being asked. This is the single fastest way to go from new person to person who is relied upon.

Weeks ten to thirteen — start saying what you think in reviews. Politely, and with a reason. The transition from doing tasks to having opinions is the actual promotion, and it happens long before the title does.

The mistake I see most: spending ninety days trying to look competent. Nobody expects you to be competent yet. They are watching whether you are learning at a rate that will get you there.

elements.content:
My test passed. Then failed. Then passed again. I didn't change a single line. 🙃

It isn't haunted. It's flaky, and flaky tests are worse than no tests because they teach the team to ignore red builds.

🔍 The usual suspects 
⏱️ Hard waits: sleep(5000) is a guess, not a wait 
🧪 Shared test data: two tests edit the same user 
🎯 Brittle locators: div > div:nth-child(7) 
🔀 Order dependency: a test only passes if another one runs first 
🌐 Real third-party calls: someone else's slow API fails your build 
🕐 Time and timezone: tests that break at midnight or at month-end

🛠️ How to fix them 
✅ Wait for a state (visible, enabled, response received), never for a fixed time 
✅ Give every test its own data, created via API and cleaned up afterwards 
✅ Use stable locators: data-testid, role, label 
✅ Make each test independent so it can run alone, in any order, in parallel 
✅ Mock what you don't own 
✅ Use a fixed clock and timezone in tests

🧭 My approach to keeping a suite stable
1️⃣ Detect: track the pass rate per test, and run new tests 10–20× before merging (--repeat-each) 
2️⃣ Quarantine: move flaky tests out of the blocking pipeline instead of deleting them 
3️⃣ Fix the root cause: use traces, videos and logs, not intuition 
4️⃣ Prevent: add flakiness checks to PR review and make "no hard waits" a team rule

⚠️ Retries are a painkiller, not a cure. If you need retries: 3 to go green, you have a bug somewhere, in the test or in the product.

Teams running parallel CI often spend days hunting flaky tests, only to discover the problem was never in the application code at all. It was in the pipeline.

When a test fails only under parallel execution and the failure mode keeps changing (foreign key violation one time, connection refused the next, a timestamp assertion off by two seconds after that), the instinct is to read the test again. Our latest article makes the case for a different instinct: stop reading the test. You are looking at a race condition in the distributed system you accidentally built.

The article walks through four specific infrastructure race conditions that only surface under parallel CI, each with a reproduction pattern and a fix. Shared databases, where two workers collide on the same Postgres instance during teardown. Port collisions, where a hardcoded port produces silent failures when a worker connects to the wrong server entirely. Container startup races, where "started" and "ready" are not the same thing, and faster CI machines make this worse by exposing the window. And clock skew, where jobs on different machines disagree on time by enough to break timestamp assertions and boundary-condition tests.

For each one, the article gives concrete, runnable code: per-worker Postgres databases stamped from a template, binding to port 0 so the OS assigns a free one, Docker Compose health checks that gate on actual readiness rather than container start, and time-injection patterns that remove wall-clock dependency entirely. The point throughout is that retrying your way past these failures just makes them invisible. The underlying race stays live until you address the resource sharing directly.

If your team has tests that only misbehave at high parallelism, this is worth a read.

I built 5 frameworks in less than a month. Here's what I actually learned.

1. The hard part is never generation. It's review.
Every AI test generator produces volume in seconds. testforge taught me the bottleneck was never "can it write tests?" - it's "which of these 100 should exist?" An LLM that generates 100 tests where 65% get cut hasn't helped; it's moved the work.

2. Fail rate and flakiness are not the same number.
pulse taught me this. A test that fails 100% of the time looks flaky to every naive detector. It's not - it's a regression. Stability is information. Direction doesn't matter.

3. A retry policy isn't a number.
rely taught me that retries: 3 on everything is a shrug, not a strategy. A real bug should retry 0 times. A flake should retry 3. A drifted locator needs re-resolution, not another attempt with the same selector.

4. Acting on a wrong answer is worse than not acting.
culprit taught me this. An RCA tool that posts to Slack immediately is right 80% of the time and a liability 100% of the time. The gate is the product.

5. Flat structures hide information.
oath taught me this. Every API tool sees an OpenAPI spec as a list of endpoints. A dependency graph shows you that POST /auth/login feeds 11 downstream consumers. Same data. Different shape. Different answer.
